extracted.intended_audience: researchers preparing and submitting manuscripts to peer-reviewed journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors to pass an editor's initial screening (avoid desk rejection), diagnose why a manuscript was desk‑rejected, and choose next steps or a better target journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desk rejection means an editor rejected your manuscript without sending it to external peer review; the paper never left the editor's desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a typical submission the paper goes through two stages: the editor's initial screening (the desk), then external peer review. The editor usually reads title and abstract and maybe skims the paper, then decides not to send it on. Decisions often arrive within a few days to two weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish desk rejection vs. peer review rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Desk rejection is a fast, single-editor decision often with a generic 'not suitable' message; peer review rejection follows months of external evaluation with detailed reviewer feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desk rejection: happens in days, one person's decision, usually about fit/scope/framing, no reviewer comments, you can resubmit elsewhere immediately. Peer review rejection: takes 2–6 months, based on expert evaluation, gives detailed feedback about scientific quality and methods, and usually requires revision before resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience and scope do not match the journal; you submitted to a journal that publishes different types or levels of work than yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to check: Read 10 recent papers from the journal (e.g., 10 papers from the last two issues). If yours doesn't fit the same scope and ambition, retarget and rewrite the submission package. Best response after desk rejection for this reason: retarget and rewrite the package to a journal whose recent output matches your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty isn't clear
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor cannot tell what is new about your work from the title and abstract; the advance is buried or undersold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes: Put your novel contribution in the first sentence of the abstract (lead with the contribution). Rewrite title, abstract, and cover letter so the advance is obvious within 1–2 minutes of reading. Emphasize what matters to the target journal's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence does not feel secure enough — examples include underpowered studies, missing controls, inappropriate statistical tests, or a methods section that's too vague to evaluate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to fix: Repair controls, statistics, or reporting before resubmitting. Have someone outside your group read the methods section; if they can't replicate the study from what you wrote, add detail. Incomplete or flawed methods often mean 'no next journal yet' until fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor writing or presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor cannot understand what you did or what you found due to dense paragraphs, unclear figures, jargon-heavy prose, or poor English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes: Rebuild figures, tighten the writing, reduce jargon, and get editing help (professional or from colleagues). Even native speakers need editorial help; editors won't send poorly written papers to reviewers because it wastes time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission is incomplete or careless: missing ethics approval statement, no data availability statement, wrong reference format, missing figure legends, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes: Read the journal's 'Guide for Authors' and run the author checklist line by line (ethics approval, data availability, reference format, figure specs). Small omissions signal carelessness and are easy to prevent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiming too high
rubrics_metrics.description: The work is sound but the journal's significance bar is higher than the data; a well-done but modest study doesn't meet flagship-journal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes: Move down one tier (not several), be honest about where your paper fits, and ask a senior colleague for a realistic assessment. Choose a reputable field journal that rewards completeness over headline breadth when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal does not need this paper now: someone else published something similar, there's just been a special issue on your topic, or the field has moved on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes: You can't fully prevent timing problems, but checking the journal's recent publications before submitting helps. If timing is the reason for desk rejection, submit elsewhere quickly to avoid staleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the desk-rejection reason changes next-target choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Different desk-rejection causes imply different next journals or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping in brief: Broad-scope mismatch → target a strong specialty or companion journal; Incremental advance → target a reputable field journal with lower novelty bar; Incomplete methods/controls → fix evidence issues before resubmitting (no good next journal until fixed); Presentation/framing → front-end revision can allow submission to a comparable journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the rejection carefully (diagnosis step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even brief rejection emails often contain clues about why the paper was declined (e.g., 'not within our scope', 'insufficient novelty', 'not of sufficient interest to our broad readership').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precise wording to diagnose wrong_journal, novelty, or interest-level problems and plan appropriate next steps instead of guessing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't appeal (usually)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals of desk rejections rarely succeed (less than ~5% success rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend the weeks you would use to craft an appeal on selecting a better target or improving the manuscript, unless the editor clearly misunderstood the paper and you can explain the misunderstanding in two concise sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't just resubmit the same paper elsewhere (pause and revise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately resubmitting unchanged to another journal repeats the same errors and wastes time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take 24–48 hours, then reread and revise your abstract and cover letter with fresh eyes. Make novelty obvious, improve framing, and fix any presentation issues before resubmitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-submission checklist / readiness filters
rubrics_metrics.description: A short set of pre-submission checks that prevent the most common desk-rejection patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these filters before submitting: 1) Match the journal's recent output (read ~10 recent papers). 2) Lead with the contribution in the abstract (novel finding in first one-two sentences). 3) Audit methods independently (ask an outsider if they could replicate). 4) Run the journal's author checklist line by line (ethics, data statements, figure specs). 5) Get a blunt read on clarity (if a colleague outside your subfield can't summarize the abstract in two sentences, revise). These catch scope mismatch, missing elements, and presentation problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-desk-rejection action steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A step-by-step plan for what to do immediately after receiving a desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Read the rejection carefully and infer the likely reason. Step 2: Don't appeal in most cases. Step 3: Wait 24–48 hours, then revise the title/abstract/cover letter (don't resubmit unchanged). Step 4: Choose a better target based on the inferred reason (move down one tier or target specialty journals as appropriate). Step 5: Strengthen framing (emphasize what's relevant to the new journal's audience). Step 6: Submit again; persistence and willingness to improve are key. Also consider getting outside feedback or a pre-submission review to check framing and fit.
